t.6.38.1: Seeing her husband struck down, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa as well, Sītā, wasted by grief, lamented bitterly and piteously.
t.6.38.3: Those who said of me that I would be the chief queen of one who offers sacrifices and the wife of one who performs sacrificial sessions, all of them, now that Rāma is slain, are today ignorant men and speakers of falsehood.
t.6.38.2: The readers of auspicious marks who told me, 'You will be a mother of sons and never a widow,' now that Rāma is slain, have all proven ignorant in this matter and speakers of falsehood.
t.6.38.4: Those who said of me, 'You are the wife of a heroic king,' and 'She is fortunate,' all of them today, now that Rāma is slain, stand revealed as ignorant men and speakers of falsehood.
t.6.38.5: Those twice-born astrologers who, within my hearing, declared me auspicious, now that Rāma is slain, have all today proven ignorant and speakers of falsehood.
t.6.38.6: These, surely, are the lotus marks on the feet by which, it is said, women are consecrated to sovereign rule together with their husbands, the lords of men.
t.6.38.7: Those inauspicious marks by which women deprived of good fortune come to widowhood, I do not see on myself, though I search, I whose auspicious marks have been rendered void.
t.6.38.8: These lotus marks, declared in the science of bodily signs to hold true for women, have today, with Rāma slain, become false for me.
t.6.38.9: My hair is fine, even and dark, and my eyebrows do not meet; my shanks are rounded and free of hair, and my teeth are set close together.
t.6.38.10: My eyes, reaching to the temples, my hands, my feet, my ankles and my thighs are full and well-formed; my nails are rounded and glossy, and my fingers are even.
t.6.38.11: These breasts of mine are full and close together, with sunken nipples; my navel is deep and its surrounds are raised, and my sides and chest are well-rounded.
t.6.38.13: My hands and feet bear the full mark of the barley-grain, are without gaps between the fingers and toes, and are of fine colour; and those who read the signs on maidens have known me as one with a gentle smile.
t.6.38.12: My complexion is like a gem and the hairs on my body are soft; they told me that I, firmly endowed with the twelve, bore auspicious marks.
t.6.38.14: The brāhmaṇas, skilled in settled conclusions, declared that I would be consecrated to sovereignty together with my husband; all that has now been made false.
t.6.38.15: Having cleared Janasthāna and obtained news of me, and having crossed the unshakable ocean, the two brothers have been slain in a cow's hoofprint.
t.6.38.16: Did not the two Rāghavas obtain the Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Aindra and Vāyavya weapons, and the Brahmaśiras as well?
t.6.38.17: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, equal to Vāsava, my protectors, have been struck down in battle by one who, through magic, remained unseen, and I am left without a protector.
t.6.38.18: For no enemy who has come within the range of Rāghava's sight in battle could return alive, even if he were as swift as thought.
t.6.38.19: Nothing is too heavy a burden for Time, and Kṛtānta, the Ender of all, is hard indeed to conquer, since Rāma lies here with his brother, struck down in battle.
t.6.38.20: I do not grieve so much for my slain husband, nor for Lakṣmaṇa, nor for myself, nor even for my mother, as I grieve for my wretched mother-in-law.
t.6.38.21: For she constantly thinks of him returned, his vow fulfilled: "When shall I see Sītā, and Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa?"
t.6.38.22: To her, as she lamented, the rākṣasī Trijaṭā said: "Do not give way to despair, O queen; this husband of yours is alive."
t.6.38.24: For when their lord has been slain, the faces of warriors in battle are not filled with rage and eager with delight.
t.6.38.23: And I will tell you the reasons, great and fitting, which show, O queen, that these two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are alive.
t.6.38.26: For an army whose chief heroes have been slain, its spirit crushed and its effort spent, drifts aimlessly in battle like a ship on the water whose helm has been lost.
t.6.38.25: O Vaidehī, this celestial aerial chariot, known by the name Puṣpaka, would not bear you if these two had lost their lives.
t.6.38.27: But this army, unbewildered, undismayed and full of vigour, guards the two Kākutsthas, who were overcome in battle by magic.
t.6.38.28: So be fully reassured by these inferences that herald happiness, and see the two Kākutsthas unslain. I tell you this out of affection.
t.6.38.29: Never before have I spoken an untruth, nor shall I ever speak one. Because of your virtuous conduct and gentle, pleasing nature, you have entered my heart.
t.6.38.30: These two cannot be conquered in battle even by the gods and asuras together with Indra; having seen their faces, I have made this known to you.
t.6.38.31: And observe calmly this very great sign, O Maithilī: though both of these are unconscious, their splendour does not depart from them at all.
t.6.38.32: Generally, in men whose vitality has departed and whose span of life is spent, an extreme distortion appears in their faces as they are beheld.
t.6.38.33: Give up your grief, your sorrow and your bewilderment, O daughter of Janaka. As for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, it is not possible that they should be without life today.
t.6.38.34: Having heard her words, Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, who resembled a daughter of the gods, joined her palms in reverence and said this: "So be it."
t.6.38.35: Turning back that aerial chariot Puṣpaka, swift as thought, Trijaṭā brought the grief-stricken Sītā back into Laṅkā itself.
t.6.38.36: Then, having descended from the Puṣpaka together with Trijaṭā, she was led back into the Aśoka grove itself by the rākṣasīs.
t.6.38.37: Having entered that pleasure-ground of the lord of the rākṣasas, thick with clusters of many trees, Sītā looked about and, thinking of the two princes, sank into the deepest despair.
